regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 55.9","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY and PMI Composite at 55.9 look unambiguous — until you note that core sector growth slipped to 4.8% YoY from 5.0%, and passenger vehicle sales decelerated for two consecutive months to 7.9% YoY from 26.1%. The quality of growth is narrowing: IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY is doing the heavy lifting, but that is investment-led, not consumption-led. Invert the bull case: if the capex cycle is crowding out consumption credit (credit card growth at just 3.6% YoY, 25th percentile), the multiplier effect on household income is weaker than the headline suggests.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 5.54% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY has moved 230 bps in two months (from 3.21%), driven by food at 7.74% YoY and fuel at 22.93% YoY — the latter at its 95th percentile historically. Core CPI at 3.9% YoY is the number the RBI actually watches, and it is not alarming — yet. The trap: if Brent holds above $95/bbl and the INR weakens further from 94.34, imported inflation feeds into core with a two-quarter lag. The RBI's own inflation forecast of 5.1% YoY is already above the 4% midpoint target; the next upward revision will be harder to communicate as transitory.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.4% YoY; CD ratio 81%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.4% YoY (80th percentile) against deposit growth at 17.8% YoY keeps the CD ratio at 81% — elevated but easing from 83% two months ago. The stress is migrating: NBFC credit accelerating to 15.8% YoY while corporate bond issuance sits at ₹18,700 cr / month (4th percentile) means NBFCs are rationing wholesale funding and leaning harder on bank lines. The historical precedent is instructive: the last time the CD ratio sustained above 80% with credit growing faster than deposits, the RBI responded with risk-weight increases on unsecured lending within three quarters. The incentive to act is building.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is unchanged, and the RBI's stated stance is data-dependent. The real rate — repo minus headline CPI — has compressed to -29 bps, which is accommodative by any measure. With the RBI's own inflation forecast at 5.1% YoY and food inflation at 7.74% YoY, the case for a cut has evaporated; the question is whether the case for a hike is building. A US 10Y at 5.1% yield and INR at 94.34 (89th percentile) narrow the RBI's room to stay passive — FX defence and inflation management are now pulling in the same direction: hold, or tighten.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY for the third consecutive month of acceleration, with capacity utilisation rising to 77.4% of capacity (68th percentile), is the most credible signal of a genuine investment upcycle. The inversion: capacity utilisation typically needs to cross 80% before private capex becomes self-sustaining — at 77.4%, the cycle is real but not yet self-reinforcing. Bank credit to industry at 18.2% YoY and services at 24.3% YoY confirm the investment is being funded; the risk is that funding costs rise faster than project IRRs if the RBI is forced to tighten.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹203521 cr/mo; PV 7.9% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,03,521 cr / month (74th percentile) is solid, but the composition matters: two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY signal rural recovery, while passenger vehicle sales at 7.9% YoY (decelerating from 26.1%) and commercial vehicle sales at 12.6% YoY (falling two months) suggest urban and freight demand is softening. The GST number itself may flatter: at 74th percentile, it reflects both genuine demand and ongoing formalization of the informal economy — the two are indistinguishable in the aggregate. E-commerce GMV growth at 12.4% YoY (16th percentile) is the tell: digital consumption, which skews urban and affluent, is not accelerating.","badge_label":"Stable Consumption","badge_type":"b-neu"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.4% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160 bps divergence that has widened for 2 consecutive months (17.1%→19.4% credit, 9.9%→17.8% deposits). CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits, down from 82.2% but still at 71st percentile historically. NBFC credit accelerating at 15.8% YoY (up from 10% YoY prior), now at 56th percentile. Corporate bond issuance at 18,700 ₹ cr / month — a 4th percentile low, signalling NBFCs are rationing wholesale funding.","implication":"RBI will face pressure to either hike rates to attract deposits or relax liquidity conditions. Overweight private banks with CASA ratios >45% — they'll poach deposits from smaller lenders. Avoid NBFCs with wholesale funding >30% of liabilities; their funding costs will spike. Watch for RBI to signal a rate cut by Q2 FY27 to ease deposit stress. Position for a 50-75 bps rate cut cycle starting H2 FY27.","pct_10y":71,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 71st percentile is elevated but not extreme. Historically, ratios >85% preceded NBFC stress (2018-19) and forced RBI intervention. Current divergence is manageable but trending toward stress territory.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Cycle Accelerating Into Cycle Peak","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (latest), up from 16.1% YoY prior — 3rd consecutive month of acceleration. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (up from 75.6%), now at 68th percentile. Core sector growth at 4.8% YoY (down from 5% YoY) but still at 50th percentile. India credit to industry at 18.2% YoY (up from 7% YoY), now at 73rd percentile; services credit at 24.3% YoY (up from 10.3%), at 73rd percentile. Vehicle credit at 19.7% YoY (up from 8.7%), at 67th percentile.","implication":"Capex cycle is in mid-expansion, not peak. Overweight capital goods, cement, and steel stocks — order books are filling. Favour PSU capex plays (railways, power) over private capex, as government spending is more visible. Avoid consumer discretionary; capex spending is crowding out consumption. Position for 12-18 month capex tailwind; expect IIP capital goods to sustain 14-18% growth through Q3 FY27.","pct_10y":68,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is mid-cycle; historically, peaks occur at 80-82%. This suggests 2-3 quarters of capex acceleration remain before saturation.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Inflows Hit 95th Percentile, Affluent Money Entering","data_text":"SIP inflows at 32,490 ₹ cr / month (latest), rising 3 consecutive months (29,845→31,961→32,297→32,490). SIP accounts at 10.0646 mn (down from 10.45 mn prior), but SIP AUM at 17.86 ₹ lakh cr (up from 16.64 ₹ lakh cr), now at 92nd percentile. Average SIP AUM per account rising: SIP AUM ÷ accounts = 17.74 ₹ lakh cr per mn accounts vs prior 15.9 ₹ lakh cr per mn accounts — a 11.6% increase in average ticket size. Equity MF net inflows at 38,307 ₹ cr net / month (up from 29,329 ₹ cr net / month), at 85th percentile. DII equity net at 51,829 ₹ cr net / month (96th percentile) vs FII equity net at -49,935 ₹ cr net / month (14th percentile).","implication":"SIP growth is decelerating in account count but accelerating in AUM — affluent retail is entering, not mass retail. This is late-cycle behaviour. Overweight large-cap, dividend-paying stocks; underweight small-cap and growth. Expect SIP inflows to sustain but growth rate to decelerate to 8-10% YoY by Q3 FY27. DII dominance suggests domestic money is confident; FII outflows are a hedge against INR weakness and US rate risk. Reduce exposure to high-beta, FII-dependent names.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 95th percentile are at all-time highs. Rising average ticket size (11.6% increase) is a red flag for late-cycle retail euphoria — historically preceded market corrections by 6-12 months.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation at 95th Percentile, Import Bill Spiking","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (latest), up from 20.05% YoY prior — rising 2 consecutive months. At 95th percentile historically. Brent crude at 95.38 $/bbl (up from 91.72 $/bbl 5 months ago), at 70th percentile. WTI at 88.31 $/bbl, at 69th percentile. FAO food index at 136 index (up from 128.5 index 4 months ago), at 63rd percentile. Food inflation at 7.74% YoY (up from 3.47% YoY 2 months ago), rising 2 consecutive months. India's headline CPI at 5.54% YoY (up from 3.21% YoY 2 months ago), now at 53rd percentile.","implication":"Oil and food inflation are the primary drivers of headline CPI overshoot. RBI will struggle to cut rates while fuel inflation remains >20% YoY. Current account deficit will widen if oil stays >$95/bbl; INR depreciation pressure will persist. Hedge INR exposure; avoid long-duration bonds. Overweight energy and agri-stocks; underweight consumer staples (margin compression). Expect RBI to hold rates at 5.25% p.a. through Q2 FY27, then cut only if oil falls below $85/bbl.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is extreme. Historically, such levels preceded RBI rate hikes (2021-22) or extended pause cycles (2011-12). Current pause is unsustainable if fuel inflation persists.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"Fed Hiking, BOJ Tightening, Carry Unwind Risk","data_text":"Fed funds rate at 3.88% p.a. (up from 3.63% p.a. 3 months ago), rising 3 consecutive months, at 75th percentile. US 10Y Treasury yield at 5.1% yield (up from 4.94% yield 4 months ago), rising 4 of last 5 months, at 93rd percentile. BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (up from 0.75% p.a. 2 months ago), rising 2 consecutive months, at 100th percentile (all-time high). ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (up from 2% p.a. 2 months ago), rising 2 consecutive months, at 64th percentile. US PMI composite at 58.4 index (up from 50.3 index 2 months ago), at 80th percentile. DXY at 103.421 index (up from 102.2 index 4 months ago), rising 4 of last 5 months, at 60th percentile.","implication":"Global central banks are diverging: Fed and BOJ tightening, ECB neutral. This is a carry unwind environment — JPY strength will pressure INR and emerging market currencies. US rates at 93rd percentile (10Y) are a headwind for equity valuations globally. Reduce leverage; hedge INR/JPY exposure. Avoid high-beta EM assets; overweight developed market bonds (US 10Y at 5.1% is attractive). Expect EM currency weakness to persist through Q2 FY27. Position for a 50-75 bps INR depreciation vs USD.","pct_10y":93,"pct_note":"US 10Y at 93rd percentile is near cycle highs. Historically, such levels preceded EM currency crises (2013 taper tantrum, 2018 EM selloff). Current environment is similar: Fed tightening + BOJ hiking = carry unwind.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Weakening Into 89th Percentile, Reserves Pressure","data_text":"INR/USD at 94.34 ₹ (up from 93.46 ₹ 2 months ago), at 89th percentile. FII equity net at -49,935 ₹ cr net / month (14th percentile), indicating sustained outflows. DII equity net at 51,829 ₹ cr net / month (96th percentile), offsetting FII outflows. India's current account deficit is widening due to oil imports (fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY) and weak services exports (services credit growth at 24.3% YoY is domestic, not export-driven). US 10Y Treasury at 5.1% yield (93rd percentile) is attracting capital away from India. India VIX at 15.495 index (47th percentile), suggesting complacency despite INR weakness.","implication":"RBI is likely intervening to defend INR, but reserves are under pressure. INR will likely weaken to 95-96 ₹/USD by Q2 FY27 if oil stays >$90/bbl and US rates remain elevated. Hedge INR exposure via forwards or options; avoid long-dated INR liabilities. Overweight exporters (IT, pharma, textiles) — INR weakness is a tailwind. Underweight importers (oil, metals). Expect RBI to maintain a defensive stance on INR, limiting rate cuts even if inflation moderates.","pct_10y":89,"pct_note":"INR at 89th percentile is near 10-year highs in weakness. Historically, such levels preceded RBI intervention cycles (2013, 2018) and capital controls discussions. Current level is unsustainable without policy action.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Collapsed, GCC Thesis Broken","data_text":"Office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter (latest), down from 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter 2 quarters ago — a 79% collapse. Office vacancy at 13.4% vacant (down from 14.5% prior), suggesting supply-side tightness, not demand strength. Yet Nifty IT is flat at 25,144.3 index (85th percentile), and IT services credit growth at 24.3% YoY (73rd percentile) is accelerating. Disconnect: office absorption is cratering while IT credit is surging. This suggests IT companies are borrowing for capex (data centres, cloud infra) and M&A, NOT for office expansion. Global capability centres (GCCs) are the marginal buyer of office space, but they're consolidating footprints, not expanding. Commercial real estate (office) is decoupling from IT services as a proxy. Retail mall vacancy at 11.15% vacant (37th percentile) is stable, suggesting consumer discretionary is resilient. But office absorption collapse signals IT services are shifting to asset-light models (outsourcing, cloud, automation).","implication":"IT services stocks are NOT a play on office real estate recovery — they're a play on capex and M&A cycles. Overweight IT capex beneficiaries (data centre REITs, cloud infra plays) and underweight traditional IT services on valuation. Office REITs (Embassy, Mindspace, Brookfield) are at 57-58th percentile valuations but face structural headwinds from remote work and GCC consolidation. Avoid office REITs; overweight data centre and logistics REITs. IT services credit growth at 24.3% YoY is NOT a bullish signal for office demand — it's a signal of capex intensity and margin pressure from automation. Reduce IT services exposure; rotate into IT infrastructure and cloud plays.","pct_10y":4,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 4th percentile is a 10-year low. This is a structural shift, not a cyclical dip. GCC consolidation and remote work adoption are permanent headwinds for office real estate. Historical precedent: 2008-09 financial crisis saw similar office absorption collapses that took 5+ years to recover.","is_surprise":true}

{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP Headline, Narrowing Base — Capex Carries What Consumption Cannot

The facts:

  • India GDP at 7.8% YoY with PMI Composite at 55.9 — both above 50th-percentile historically — signal expansion, but IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY is doing the work consumption should be doing.
  • Passenger vehicle sales decelerated to 7.9% YoY (from 26.1% YoY two months ago); commercial vehicle sales fell to 12.6% YoY for the second consecutive month — freight and urban demand are losing altitude.
  • Two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY signal rural recovery is real, but e-commerce GMV growth at 12.4% YoY (16th percentile) says the urban, digital consumer is not accelerating.
  • But core sector growth slipped to 4.8% YoY from 5.0% — the infrastructure backbone of the capex story is not keeping pace with the headline.

The tension: The GDP print is investment-led, not consumption-led. A capex cycle that outruns household income growth eventually exhausts itself — capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity is not yet the 80%-plus threshold that historically triggers self-sustaining private investment.

Bottom line: Watch capacity utilisation: a print above 80% of capacity in the next quarter would confirm the capex cycle is self-reinforcing; below, it remains policy-dependent and vulnerable to funding cost increases.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US 10Y at 93rd Percentile — Every EM Carry Trade Has a Maturity Date

The facts:

  • US 10Y Treasury at 5.1% yield (93rd percentile), rising four of the last five months — the highest real borrowing cost in a decade, tightening global financial conditions without a single Fed meeting.
  • Fed Funds Rate at 3.88% p.a. (75th percentile), rising three consecutive months; BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, all-time high) — the two anchors of global carry are both moving against EM.
  • US GDP SAAR accelerated to 3.4% SAAR from 2.2% — the growth that justifies higher-for-longer rates is arriving, which removes the Fed's incentive to pivot.
  • But China GDP at 4.4% YoY (46th percentile) and China CPI at 0.9% YoY mean the commodity reflation that would offset EM pressure is not coming from Beijing.

The tension: DM growth is re-accelerating precisely as DM rates hit multi-decade highs — the combination that historically drains EM capital flows. India's $680 bn reserve cushion buys time; it does not change the direction.

Bottom line: If US 10Y crosses 5.25% yield, expect FII outflows to accelerate beyond the current ₹49,935 cr net / month — hedge INR exposure accordingly.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

DII Absorption at 96th Percentile — Domestic Liquidity Plugging a Foreign Exit

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (95th percentile), rising three consecutive months — average SIP AUM per account up 11.6% YoY to ₹17.74 lakh cr per mn accounts, signalling affluent money entering, not mass retail.
  • DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr net / month (96th percentile) is absorbing FII equity outflows of ₹49,935 cr net / month (14th percentile) almost exactly — the market is balanced on a knife-edge of domestic conviction.
  • But MF AUM fell to ₹82.64 lakh cr from ₹87.08 lakh cr — mark-to-market erosion is quietly shrinking the pool that funds DII absorption.
  • Corporate bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr / month (4th percentile) signals NBFCs are rationing wholesale funding — the credit channel is tightening from the bottom up.

The tension: Domestic liquidity looks robust in flow terms but fragile in stock terms: MF AUM is falling even as SIP inflows rise, meaning market returns are not compounding the base. If equity markets correct, SIP redemptions accelerate and DII absorption capacity shrinks simultaneously.

Bottom line: Watch MF AUM: a sustained print below ₹82 lakh cr would signal mark-to-market pressure is outpacing SIP inflows and DII absorption capacity is eroding.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

REITs Pricing Office Collapse; Residential Bifurcating by City and Ticket

The facts:

  • NRI buying is FALLING — NRI share of residential purchases at 18% (down from 15% prior print, but NRI share within premium/luxury at 32% remains elevated) — remittances at $155.1 bn (14.5% YoY) sustain the flow, but INR at 94.34 reduces rupee-denominated returns for dollar earners.
  • Premium segment (₹80 lakh–₹1.5 cr) is oversupplied by 3 pp (34% of launches vs 31% of sales); Hyderabad leads with sales up 15% YoY and launches up 120% YoY — a supply surge that will test absorption within 28 months of unsold inventory.
  • Office REITs — Embassy at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, Brookfield at ₹263/unit — have fallen 13–31% from prior prints, pricing the office absorption collapse to 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter from 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter two quarters ago.
  • But Nifty 50 at 25,144 (85th percentile) and Bank Nifty at 61,034 (100th percentile) have not repriced the credit and FX risks embedded in the macro.

The tension: Equities are pricing the capex and credit growth story; REITs are pricing the office demand collapse. Both cannot be right about the same economy — the divergence resolves either through an equity correction or a REIT recovery, and the office absorption data favours the former.

Bottom line: Avoid office REITs until absorption recovers above 10 mn sq ft / quarter; in equities, hedge Bank Nifty at 100th percentile against the credit-deposit and FX risks that are not yet priced.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Four Risks, One Trigger — US Yields Are the Keystone

The facts:

  • US 10Y at 5.1% yield (93rd percentile) — if it crosses 5.25% yield, EM carry unwinds accelerate, FII outflows exceed ₹50,000 cr net / month, and INR tests 96+. Probability: high; impact: severe.
  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) with Brent at $95.38/bbl — every $10/bbl adds ~$15 bn to India's annual import bill, widening CAD by ~40 bps and feeding CPI with a two-quarter lag. Probability: medium; impact: high.
  • CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits with corporate bond issuance at a 4th-percentile ₹18,700 cr / month — NBFC funding stress is the most likely trigger for a macro-prudential response (risk-weight hike) that would reprice bank credit. Probability: medium; impact: medium-high.
  • BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, all-time high) — yen carry unwind is not priced in India VIX at 15.5 (47th percentile); a disorderly BOJ move would hit EM liquidity within 30–60 days. Probability: low; impact: severe.

The tension: All four risks share a common transmission: a stronger dollar and higher global rates compress India's external financing cushion simultaneously. The RBI's $680 bn reserve buffer is the margin of safety — but it is being tested on multiple fronts at once.

Bottom line: Watch US 10Y yield this week: a close above 5.2% yield is the threshold that triggers the FII outflow, INR depreciation, and imported inflation chain — the single number that connects every risk on this list.

"}
